Al-Naẓẓām seems to explain this through motion.

A being that exists, or lies hidden, within another being of the same kind—a mineral within mineral matter, a plant within a plant, and so on—undergoes a certain movement and then “appears” from where it had been hidden.
But this movement is not a transfer from one place to another.
It is movement in the sense of change: the being enters a new state.
Al-Naẓẓām therefore places this kind of movement under the category known in Aristotelian logic as position.
“Movement, for al-Naẓẓām, is the beginning of some change, just as the philosophers speak of quantity, quality, position, where”—that is, place—“when”—that is, time—“and the other categories.”
This follows from al-Naẓẓām’s broader view of movement.
He says that all human actions are movements.
There is no real state of rest.
What we call rest is itself a movement of resistance or support.
The same applies to knowledge and acts of will. These too are movements of the soul.
Al-Naẓẓām therefore denies that true rest exists anywhere in the universe.
For him, the universe is nothing but movement.
In this early vision of the universe within Arab thought, we find a philosophical view closely connected with his earlier idea that material beings remain hidden and then emerge.
That theory too contains an advanced philosophical insight that pushes boldly into the metaphysical framework of Muʿtazilite thought.

And if we place beside it another doctrine introduced by al-Naẓẓām—the denial of the indivisible particle, meaning his belief that matter can be divided without limit—we can see a real connection and coherence in his thinking.
This allows us to identify a materialist tendency in al-Naẓẓām’s thought.
Its historical and intellectual importance is not reduced by the fact that it still appears within a metaphysical and idealist framework.
That framework belonged to the historical conditions of al-Naẓẓām’s age and society.
It would be neither realistic nor scientific to demand that representatives of Arab-Islamic thought living under those historical conditions should have escaped that framework completely.
7 — The Source of Al-Naẓẓām’s Idea of Latency and Emergence
Historians of Islamic sects, as well as later scholars of Arab philosophy, tried to identify the source from which al-Naẓẓām took these theoretical ideas about nature and God.
We have already seen that al-Shahrastānī traces them back to the philosophers.
He gives us two clues about which philosophers he means.
The first is his reference to the categories of quantity, quality, position, place, and time.
These are categories of Aristotelian logic.
This suggests that al-Shahrastānī is thinking of the Greek philosophers generally and Aristotle in particular.
His second clue comes in his discussion of al-Naẓẓām’s claim that all beings were created at once.

“took this doctrine from the philosophers who taught latency and emergence. He always tended more toward the doctrines of the natural philosophers than toward those of the metaphysicians.” (al-Milal, p. 58)
This points us toward a clear original source among the Greek natural philosophers: the doctrine of Anaxagoras.
Al-Naẓẓām’s theory that all beings were created at once led him to his theory of latency and emergence.
This is not far from Anaxagoras’s principle that “everything is in everything.”
Anaxagoras described the elements involved in this process as homoeomeries.

If we connect al-Naẓẓām’s theory of latency and emergence with his other theory of endlessly divisible parts—the denial of an indivisible particle—we can compare both ideas with Anaxagoras’s belief that the world contains an infinite number of elements from which all existing things are formed.
Different combinations of these seeds produce different things.
This is why, according to Anaxagoras, everything resembles other things to some degree.
And precisely because of this underlying similarity, one thing can change into another.
Something is described as black rather than white, for example, not because blackness contains absolutely no whiteness, but because blackness predominates in it even though whiteness is also present.

The comparison between these two ideas in al-Naẓẓām and Anaxagoras’s theory of “seeds” gives some support to al-Shahrastānī’s suggestion that al-Naẓẓām took the idea of latency and emergence in creation from the Greek natural philosophers.
Al-Shahrastānī does not identify a particular Greek school in the passage just quoted.
But elsewhere, when he discusses “the view of Anaxagoras,” he becomes more specific.
“He was the first to teach latency and emergence.”
“He affirmed the actual existence of an infinite body made up of similar parts.”

It is worth noting in passing that al-Shahrastānī’s account of Anaxagoras on latency and emergence comes surprisingly close to the core of Anaxagoras’s doctrine as it is known from the history of Greek philosophy.

Once we make this comparison between al-Naẓẓām’s theory and that of Anaxagoras—and in our view the comparison rests on solid ground—there is little reason to accept the claims of other historians and scholars who trace al-Naẓẓām’s theory of creation to Stoic influence.
The Stoic idea of the “seminal cause” does not appear in al-Naẓẓām nearly as clearly as Anaxagoras’s theory does.
On this point, we can therefore disagree with Abū Rīda in one respect while agreeing with him in another.
Abū Rīda denies that al-Naẓẓām was influenced either by Stoicism or by Anaxagoras.
He argues instead that al-Naẓẓām’s theory of creation was an original idea that grew directly out of the Muʿtazilite principle of divine unity.
We disagree with him when he denies the influence of Anaxagoras’s theory of latency and emergence.
The resemblance is too clear for serious research to dismiss or ignore.
At the same time, we can agree with Abū Rīda that al-Naẓẓām’s theory of creation also grows out of his own Muʿtazilite commitment to divine unity.
There is no contradiction between saying that the theory was rooted in Muʿtazilite thought and saying that al-Naẓẓām was influenced by Anaxagoras.
Al-Naẓẓām clearly remained committed to the Muʿtazilite principle of divine unity. There is no doubt that this principle remained a foundation of his thought.
But he was also a thinker who had absorbed the culture of his age with unusual breadth and depth.
He could hardly have avoided drawing on the many intellectual traditions with which Arab-Islamic thought had come into contact.
Nor could he have avoided enriching his own doctrine through the new philosophical traditions he encountered and engaged with.
This allowed him to develop his ideas and bring his philosophical thinking into closer contact with the intellectual world of his time.
None of this means that he deliberately set out to borrow particular ideas in a direct or mechanical way.
A thinker who has deeply absorbed several intellectual traditions naturally allows them to enrich the concepts he already holds.
How far this happens depends on his theoretical awareness and on his ability to draw new conclusions that remain consistent with the basic ideas formed by the conditions of his own society and age.
Here we are satisfied with establishing that al-Naẓẓām was influenced by Anaxagoras in those questions that were connected with his Muʿtazilite principle of divine unity.
But we continue to affirm the basic principle on which this entire study rests:
The first source of every major path taken in the historical development of Arab-Islamic thought was the objective reality of the developing Arab-Islamic society itself.

For this reason, we also reaffirm that Muʿtazilite thought continued along an intellectual line reaching back to the political struggles of the earliest period of Islam, and that the five principles on which Muʿtazilite doctrine was founded represent a continuation of the ideas of those who came before them along the same line, especially thinkers who lived around the time of Wāṣil ibn ʿAṭāʾ, the founder of the Muʿtazilite school. These included Maʿbad al-Juhanī, Ghaylān al-Dimashqī and ʿAmr al-Maqṣūṣ among the Qadarites; Jahm ibn Ṣafwān among the advocates of predestination; al-Jaʿd ibn Dirham, who helped lay the foundations for rational interpretation of Islamic texts; Abū Hāshim ʿAbd Allāh ibn Muḥammad ibn al-Ḥanafiyya, from whom Ibn al-Murtaḍā says Wāṣil ibn ʿAṭāʾ learned; al-Ḥasan al-Baṣrī, Wāṣil’s teacher; and ʿAmr ibn ʿUbayd, Wāṣil’s companion at the beginning of the Muʿtazilite movement.

But none of this should make us forget that the relationship between thought and the real world does not always remain direct or mechanical. As thought rises to the level of abstract concepts, its reflection of reality no longer simply reproduces reality in its immediate form. Thought gains a new degree of relative independence. It also gains the ability to act back on the real world. In other words, thought is both influenced by reality and capable of influencing it; it does not remain purely passive.
From this we must draw three conclusions about the influence of outside cultures on Arab-Islamic thought.
First, that influence was real. It genuinely happened, and no scientific approach to history can deny it.

Second, Arab-Islamic thought did not simply absorb these cultures passively. It also acted on them. It added to them, criticized them, rejected what deserved to be rejected, and developed what was capable of further development.

Third, no matter how powerful or rich the influence of other world cultures may have been, it could not cut Arab-Islamic thought off from its own roots. Nor could it erase the original relationship between intellectual activity and the social soil from which it grew, together with the particular conditions of life that shaped it.
8 — The Maʿmariyya and the Idea of “Meanings”

In the Muʿtazilite discussion of God’s attributes, the attribute of “creation” takes on a new form in the thought of one of their thinkers, Maʿmar ibn ʿAbbād al-Sulamī. The Maʿmariyya, a group within the Basran Muʿtazila, were named after him.

Like the other Muʿtazilites, Maʿmar began from their principle of divine unity, which led them to deny that God has attributes separate from His essence. On this basis, he argued that God created nothing except bodies. The temporary properties that arise in bodies—the things theologians called “accidents”—are created by the bodies themselves.
Maʿmar divided these properties into two types.
Some arise naturally and necessarily. Fire produces burning, for example, and the sun produces heat.
Others arise through choice. Movement and rest, coming together and separating, are produced by living beings in the broad sense, including human beings.

Maʿmar also introduced a new idea into Muʿtazilite thought: the idea of “meanings.” His followers were therefore called the “People of Meanings.” The fact that they were known by this name shows how distinctive the idea was in Muʿtazilite history.
But what did the Maʿmariyya mean by “meanings”?
The historians of Islamic sects give us somewhat confused accounts.
Al-Shahrastānī explains Maʿmar’s position as follows:
“He said that the accidents within each kind are infinite. He also said that whenever an accident exists in something, it exists there because of a meaning that made it exist there.”

“Movement differs from rest not simply in itself, but because of a meaning that makes the two different. The same applies when one similar thing differs from another or resembles it, and when one opposite stands in opposition to another. In every case, this happens because of a meaning.”
From this text, we can understand two things.
First, Maʿmar says that the “accidents” themselves are infinite within every category.
Second, whenever a particular property appears in something, there must be a “meaning” that causes that property to appear.

Movement, for example, does not differ from rest simply by occurring. Behind that movement there is a meaning that makes it different from rest. The same applies to rest: it differs from movement because of a meaning.

Likewise, when one thing differs from another similar thing, or when the two resemble one another, there is a meaning that produces either the difference or the resemblance. The same applies to opposites. Two things stand in opposition to one another because a meaning produces that opposition.
When we turn to al-Ashʿarī, we find a fuller explanation.

According to him, Maʿmar argued that when a body moves, it moves because of a meaning, namely movement. Without this meaning, there would be no reason for that body rather than another body to be moving, and no reason for it to move at that particular moment rather than at an earlier one.

The same reasoning then has to be applied to movement itself. There must be another meaning that explains why this movement belongs to this particular moving body rather than to another one. And that meaning, in turn, exists because of another meaning behind it.

There is no complete totality made up of these meanings as if they were parts of one whole. They all arise at the same time. The meanings that have no final total are produced by the thing in which they exist. And we must therefore accept an infinite number of meanings within it. Life, for example, belongs to this particular living thing rather than another because of a meaning. That meaning exists because of another meaning, and so on without end.
Al-Khayyāṭ, one of the major Muʿtazilite thinkers and historians, gives us a much shorter version of the same idea:
“Everything moves and comes to rest because of a meaning within it. That meaning has another meaning behind it, and so on without end.”
